title: The naive framing: "does Claude always spawn a subagent?"
text: Someone assumed Claude always spawns a subagent to run a forecast. It doesn't only sometimes. So, does Claude sometimes spawn a subagent to forecast?

title: Anatomy: a skill is a folder (two scripts + SKILL.md)
text: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is forecasting a demand forecast for one SKU. Inside are two small scripts, rolling mean pi for a single item and batch days of cover pi for ranking many SKUs at once. The skill MD says which script to run and when to skip both and hand the job to a subagent instead. Two paths and flags decide

title: Mechanism: flags decide the path (Path A vs. Path B)
text: Which one. Path A, compute it yourself, a rolling mean over recent sales, but only when the horizon is two weeks or less, the SKU isn't seasonal, there's no promo next month, and nothing suggests a trend break. One script, no subagent. Path B, hand it to a forecasting subagent whenever any one of those flags flips, a longer horizon, a seasonal item, a promo, a visible trend. Why delegate there? The subagent needs 90 days of sales history to spot the pattern, and loading that much history into your own context would crowd out the rest of the task. The subagent gets its own context window instead. One more

title: Confidence＜ 0.6 - escalate; the number is an estimate, not a fact
text: Flag matters after the forecast comes back, confidence. Below zero, six, the rule downstream is escalate. Don't auto order. A low score doesn't mean the model is broken, it means a human should look before ordering. A high score doesn't guarantee the number is right, either. It just means nothing in the input suggested otherwise. And the number itself, forecast QTY, is not a fact about next month. It's what the rolling mean or the subagent's model computed from the flags it was given. Same flags, same path, same number every time. Claude picks compute it yourself

title: Carry-out
text: Or hand it to a subagent by the flags, not by guesswork. And whichever path runs, the number it returns is a computed estimate, not a fact about next month. Your turn. Paste this into

title: Your turn
text: Claude. I'm forecasting demand for product with a promotion next month, a 30-day horizon. Should you compute this yourself with a simple average or delegate it, and why? Then walk me through what confidence score you attach, and whether that's high enough to auto order or should escalate to a human instead. That's the actual test of a forecasting design.

title: Outro
text: Flags decide the path. Liam in for bear.
